https://udaipurkiran.com/andras-baka-ele.text: Budapest, August 12: Hungary’s parliament has elected András Baka, the former chief justice of the Supreme Court, as the country’s new president. The 73-year-old Baka was the sole candidate in the election and received 140 votes in a secret ballot. He was nominated by the ruling Fidesz party, which holds the necessary two-thirds parliamentary majority to elect a president without opposition support. The Fidesz party stated that Baka was chosen through a secret vote from a shortlist of three candidates. According to Hungarian law, a presidential candidate must have the support of at least one-fifth of the MPs, which equates to 40 members. As reported by the Xinhua news agency, Baka served as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights from 1991 to 2008. In 2009, he was appointed as the president of Hungary’s Supreme Court by the parliament. His term was cut short in 2011 due to judicial reforms introduced by then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s government. Following this, Baka continued to serve as a judge in Hungary’s top court. Fidesz noted that Baka has consistently defended the rule of law, judicial independence, and the separation of powers. The term of former president László Sólyom ended at midnight on July 20, under the 17th amendment of Hungary’s Fundamental Law. Currently, the Speaker of Parliament, Ágnes Varga, is serving as the acting president. Under the Fundamental Law, parliament is required to elect a new president within 30 days. Last week, a document published on the parliament’s website revealed that Fidesz leader Andrea Bocskor had appealed to include the presidential election in the agenda of a special parliamentary session scheduled for August 10-11. Fidesz also proposed holding the voting on August 11. Prime Minister Péter Szijjártó stated on Wednesday that he had met with Baka. In a Facebook post, Szijjártó described Baka as one of Hungary’s most respected experts on European law and constitutional matters, indicating that they had much to discuss. https://www.blisty.cz/art/135713-radical.text: Radical overhaul of Czech drug policies alarms experts 31. 8. 2026 / Albín Sybera Seasoned Czech and international drug and addiction experts are ringing alarm bells after Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ government dismantled the long-standing office for coordination of drug policies, signalling a sharp shift in the country’s drug policy. Addiction services providers declared an unprecedented strike on June 1 to protest the move the cabinet implemented on July 1 regardless of warnings that it could lead to a collapse of the policies which span several portfolios, including those of health, education, finances or interior. “What ends is a 20-year-long practice,” ex-national drug coordinator and renowned international expert in addiction Jindřich Vobořil said. Czech anti-drug policies have earned international respect in those two decades, and the country can boast a very low rate of HIV/AIDS rate among drug injection users of 4-15 cases a year, according to the latest national report on addictions. 50-80 people die of illegal drug and psychoactive medicaments overdoses, also a favourable figure by European comparison. Experts worry drug policies are falling prey to the populist rhetoric of the Babiš-led cabinet, which his Ano party formed with the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) and anti-green and Eurosceptic Motorists for Themselves parties. The ruling coalition has since pursued a cocktail of controversial policies under a neoliberal mantra of austerity which includes curtailing public media financing , targeting NGOs and purges at public environmental and human rights institutions. Vobořil continued that the Ministry of Health under Ano’s watch is signalling “a furthering of the narrative of the pharmaceutical industry”, that is, “the narrative of forbidding and prohibition where everything will be available only in the pharmacies,” Vobořil said. He explained that government changes are part of a larger tectonic shift not too different from the overhaul of drug policies seen in Hungary last year under former prime minister Viktor Orbán. Another leading Czech expert, professor Viktor Mravčík, an epidemiologist and head of research at Podané ruce addiction aid NGO and a widely published international academic, warned against the populist “normative ideology” furthered by the cabinet members and some police chiefs, which accompanies the changes in public institutions and which Mravčík described as nothing short of “a campaign against modern regulation”. Staff changes or purges? The Babiš cabinet insists that the policy changes won't have any effect on the state-funded services. “Basically, nothing is changing. The coordination stays at the Office of the Government … What changes is the transfer of the agenda. We basically take it over 1:1,” Minister of Health Adam Vojtěch said during a public hearing in July hosted by the upper chamber of the Czech parliament, the Senate, where opposition parties have a majority. It was only the 33rd such public hearing in the 30-year-old history of the Czech Senate, and one in which senators criticised government officials for not giving clear reasons for the dismantling of the existing model of drug coordination policies at a rapid pace. “The transfer [of the drug agenda] itself came from a day to day,” Helena Gherasim, chairwoman of the Council of Association of providers of addiction services (APAS), which brings together 40 Czech providers of addiction services, pointed ou. Gherasim also noted that “nearly a third of the government anti-drug experts left” following the move. The last national anti-drug coordinator, Pavel Bém, “found out about the government decision via SMS message from the head of the Office of the Government Tünde Bartha,” which Gherasim said “does not suggest it was a systematic move”. Bém, an anti-drug professional and former Prague mayor from the neoliberal Civic Democratic Party (ODS), was replaced by Dita Protopopova in June as part of the transfer of the anti-drug agenda after he was appointed to his post by the sitting government only this January, and it is as yet unclear who is to replace Bém on a long-term basis. Babiš’s Slovak-Hungarian cabinet head Bartha has long been viewed by Czech media as having an outsized informal influence over staff decisions and is suspected of co-shaping cabinet’s foreign policy and contacts with national conservatives abroad, including her participation at the Orbán-hosted CPAC conservative conference in Budapest in March this year. Moreover, Vojtěch’s words assuring of the continuity of state services contrast sharply with the continued exodus of seasoned drug professionals just days after the Senate hearing, including that of Lucia Kiššová, who was not picked to continue heading her anti-drug department after its transfer under the Ministry of Health. “It is a weakening of staff,” Mravčík said about Kiššová, who is seen as one of the most seasoned anti-drug professionals, adding that “it leaves an impression of a purge”. Underfunding of addiction services Kiššová was in charge of the anti-drug policy including oversight of grant schemes at the Office of the Government and she did not succeed in the public selection process for her post under the Ministry of Health despite Vojtěch’s pledge of the “1:1” transfer of the agenda. Kiššová’s experience “will be hard to replace” Gherasim said, noting that it is yet to be seen whether the grant schemes will be started in the autumn in time to cover addiction services next year. Gherasim and other experts are worried about the impact of staff changes on grant administration, and about lack of financing with which the sector has already been coping in recent years. They remain on alert about Vojtěch’s pledge to maintain CZK415mn (€17.17mn) in funding for next year. “Even with the CZK415mn in 2026 it was not possible to meet all the applications,” Gherasim said, adding that “at least CZK143mn were missing to cover the existing network of services”. In a statement, head of the press department at the Czech Ministry of Health Renata Povolná highlighted that “staff changes inside the state administration are a separate issue from the functioning of the addiction services network secured by individual providers”. Povolná made it clear the ministry wants to maintain the CZK415mn for the “Antidrug policy” subsidy programme and added that “we are pursuing further strengthening of financing of addiction services during the current state budget negotiations”. “We do not want to change what is functioning, but continue with the existing work and create a stable expert background for this field,” Povolná responded to a query about the ministry’s priorities. She highlighted that the ministry “does not share the presumption that the organisational transfer of the agenda itself could lead to worsening of the disponibility and quality of the addiction services” when asked about the impact of the changes on addiction services and risks in connection with higher mortality and higher rate of infectious diseases. Young lives lost Yet even the successful existing network of addiction services was described as still “significantly insufficient” by Martina Richterová Těmínová , director of the Sananim NGO, which has provided services to drug addicts and their families, including cure, care and resocialisation, since 1990. That was shortly after the 1989 fall of the communist regime in the Soviet-occupied Czechoslovakia, when modern harm reduction and control policies began to be implemented in the country to counter the inflow of drugs from abroad such as heroin. The network of addiction services “needs to be as wide as possible,” Richterová Těmínová said, explaining that the services organisations such as Sananim provide include “care of the client, therapies and social aid,” and that “it is not just about” applying legal drug substitution to clients. “We need to attend to situations when young people come and need immediate help, but there is no room for them and often this ends in loss of lives,” Richterová Těmínová says of the heartbreaking situations she deals with in her work. Although there are not yet data available for the past year, “it is clear” that in 2025 “we’d witnessed a sharp rise in the use of medical and addictive substances among youths,” which Richterová Těmínová attributes to the proliferation of social networks among youths where uncontrolled medical and drug sales flourish. There is a widespread worry in the expert community that the changes implemented by Babiš’ radical cabinet and vociferously backed by the head of the National Drug Control Centre police unit Jakub Frydrych could propel a similar emergency to the opioid crisis in the US. “If the accessibility of the substitution care and harm reduction services falls apart as a result of uncertainty surrounding its financing it alone could lead to a significant rise of deaths, to several hundred annually, and pave the way for entry of more dangerous synthetic substances on the market,” Gherasim projected. Her words were echoed by both Vobořil and Mravčík, who pointed to international academic studies, including those compiled by Vobořil, Mravčík, and Kiššová, arguing that legal regulation of psychoactive substances introduced in the Czech Republic quells illegal sales and safeguards vulnerable population. “Loss of trust in expertise” The cabinet rhetoric signals a sharp shift away from the innovative researched-based approaches to a rolling out of simplistic prohibition-based measures advocated by Frydrych, which could lead to the retraction of existing regulation of low-risk psychoactive substances and limited home cultivation of cannabis for personal use. “The rhetoric of ‘the fight against drugs’ is still alive, because it offers an easy answer to a complex problem and with exactly this it appeals to Babiš voters,” Gherasim said, noting that in expert circles such an approach “is of the previous century”. The "Power of the Law" memorial to the anti-drug unit of the Czech police outside the Police Museum in Prague. Source: Albin Sybera. Richterová Těmínová said she is sorry to see how the populist attitude to the addiction services agenda “contributed to the loss of trust in expertise” among the Czech public paralleled by the rise of “populist beerhouse politics” for which the Babiš’s fourth cabinet is also criticised after targeting environmental resort and human rights agenda . “Experience from the countries which placed bets on repression the most shows that tougher punishments do not lower the number of users, but merely push them into a riskier environment and increase the number of deaths,” Gherasim explained. She added that the “promised victory” in the fight against drugs “is not possible” because “people used the substances and will use them” and that “our task is to set up such system where people addicted to the substances would have a chance to survive, get healthy and not pose a risk to themselves or to their surroundings”. Prohibition over prevention Frydrych is a known advocate of tougher restrictions on drugs, including cannabinoid drugs, which about a third of the adult population of the country has experienced, according to the latest annual report on addiction. “From the Korund police operation we have evidence that many CBD products on the market not just damage health after unclean additions, but also often only pose as CBD while these are some yet unregulated substances,” Babiš wrote on his Facebook page on August 17. Babiš has been delivering much of his political messaging to followers on his Facebook, a dominant social platform on the Czech internet, where he called for greater “control” of “CBD as a substance” in one of his latest posts advocating for greater drug restriction. Babiš was rebuffed by Vobořil, who pointed out under the post that “the main problems are not CBD derivatives, but wholly synthetic cannabinoids, which have nothing in common with CBD,” and warned that proposals backed by Babiš could lead to CBD products becoming “unavailable for many seniors and handicapped” who use these for medical purposes. At a press conference Babiš said his cabinet will focus on Kratom but won't ban CBD, noting “it helps people, and it is part of extracts for curing”. Frydrych argued earlier that CBD is used for synthetic drugs such as HHC or Delta-8 THC, which often come to the market from China. Vobořil remains sceptical about the debated regulatory proposals of the sitting cabinet, saying she expects “people around Adam Vojtěch and Thünde Bartha” to “push ahead the prohibition policies”. He is worried that such a u-turn “will result in a mess,” explaining that existing harm reduction policies in Czechia have been successful in “pushing out heroin” for instance, while stricter prohibition policies could reinforce illegal markets from which countries hostile to Czechia such as Russia could benefit. Vobořil observed that “our neighbour Russia is threatening us with nuclear warfare, and we are mulling whether to chip in some more money for him through a grey economy”. The incoming staff replacing outgoing drug policy experts resemble “health police”, Vobořil also said. Těmínová Richterová also remains unconvinced, noting that Protopopová is “an expert on mental health, but we have no idea in what direction she would lead the drug policies”. The Bratislava native Protopopová has long been in the focus of investigative media after she filed a 2015 health report on Andrej Babiš jr. which was supposed to prevent his testimony in the Stork’s Nest subsidy embezzlement case in which Babiš sr. stands trial . Protopopová’s husband, Russian ex-cyclist Petr Protopopov was supposed to drive Babiš jr. to Russian-occupied Crimea in 2017, in what Babiš jr. later described as kidnapping, according to the Bellingcat investigation . Ideological battles or cynical business? The attention PM Babiš began to pay to drug prohibition also prompted addiction services providers to worry about stigmatisation of drug addicts. “Families of our clients remain silent, because they are stigmatised already,” Richterová Těmínová spoke of her experience, adding that what is now reinforced is “the repressive view that clients are responsible for their drug addiction”. A worker in drug addiction services who did not wish to be named criticised the government rhetoric, and said that in her experience she has rarely met an addict who was not coping with severe personal issues, including dealing with “sexual abuse from childhood”. Gherasim also pointed out a stark paradox that while the cabinet is pursuing major changes in successful anti-drug policies it remains quiet about other addictive substances which have a dire economic cost. “When it comes to the actual burden, the greatest real risk for Czech society in the long term is represented by legal substances, not illegal drugs,” she said, noting the latest report on addictions in 2025 according to which “smoking costs us CZK100bn-170bn a year, alcohol another CZK50bn-57bn, while illegal drugs cost CZK6bn-7bn” in damages. Frydrych was openly criticised by Mravčík for his June “ Drugs Are Not Norm ” op-ed published in Lidovky online news outlet in which Fridrich called for the return of “healthy reason” to anti-drug policies and that “the greatest problem is a soft vocabulary against drug risks”. Mravčík countered in his own op-ed that the “anti-drug police chief should not act as an inquisitor of the prohibition regime,” pointing to Frydrych’s “styling into a role of virtuous defender of normality in a society” and his invoking of “a chimeric world without drugs”. Turkish F-16s based at Amari Air Base in Estonia were scrambled overnight after a drone flew close to the border and entered Estonian airspace, prompting a brief air alert that was later lifted. (Turkish Air Force) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published September 1, 2026 · NATO fighter jets were scrambled and Estonian air defense units were activated early Tuesday after a drone crossed into the country during a flurry of aerial activity near the Russian border, Estonian officials said. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Tuesday that public air alerts were activated in parts of Estonia in connection with the incident, which he called “a direct consequence of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.” “NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned,” Tsahkna said, adding that the latest drone incursion in European airspace shows the need to increase pressure on Russia. Estonian Brig. Gen. Riivo Valge said military officials began tracking roughly 10 drones near the Russia-Estonia border as Ukraine carried out a large-scale drone attack against targets in western Russia. One drone initially flew from Russia toward the eastern Estonian city of Narva, prompting the military to activate ground-based air defenses and scramble NATO fighter jets from Amari Air Base. That drone turned back toward Russia, Valge said on Estonian public television. But about 30 minutes later, another drone crossed the Estonian border in the southeast and remained close to the border area, he said. “The first thing we did was activate our air defense units on the ground, and immediately after that, fighter jets took off,” Valge told public broadcaster ERR. Turkish air force fighters stationed at Amari as part of NATO’s air policing mission were scrambled in response. No drones crashed in Estonia and the NATO fighter jets did not fire their weapons, Valge said. Countries along NATO’s eastern flank have been grappling with numerous drone incursions involving both Russian and Ukrainian systems. Some NATO allies have accused Russia of using electronic warfare tactics to redirect Ukrainian drones into NATO territory. Drone activity has also emerged as a major concern in central Europe, where unmanned aircraft have repeatedly been spotted in the vicinity of U.S. and NATO bases over the past year. Last month, a drone fitted with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, prompting Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt to say that the country had reached “a new level of danger.” Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Sunday on German public television that Berlin was finalizing its response to the incident in coordination with European Union and NATO allies. Germany is on the verge of naming the suspected culprit, according to the British newspaper The Guardian. Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, has said that Moscow was behind the attempted attack in Leipzig. Some media reports have also indicated that U.S. intelligence officials believe the explosives-laden drone likely belonged to Russia. Moscow has denied responsibility for such incidents. NATO Europe John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa. Based in Stuttgart, Germany, he previously worked for newspapers in New Jersey, North Carolina and Maryland. He is a graduate of the University of Delaware. https://www.armstrongeconomics.com/inter.text: Marine Le Pen and the Nationalist Trend the Establishment Cannot Stop A new poll out of France should not be viewed as some sudden political awakening. It is confirmation that the nationalist trend we have been watching throughout Europe for years is continuing and becoming stronger. The poll places Marine Le Pen comfortably ahead in the first round of the 2027 presidential election , with roughly 36% support, far beyond any of the establishment candidates currently positioned against her. More importantly, the polling indicates that National Rally is no longer merely collecting an angry protest vote. Le Pen is increasingly competitive with, and in several scenarios ahead of, mainstream candidates in the second round where the French establishment historically united to prevent her from reaching the Élysée Palace. This is the continuation of a political trend, not the beginning of one. Brexit was part of it. Trump was part of it. Giorgia Meloni’s victory in Italy was part of it. The Freedom Party winning the largest share of the vote in Austria was part of it, as has been the extraordinary expansion of AfD in Germany. Reform UK has disrupted the old Conservative-Labour structure in Britain, while nationalist and sovereignty movements have advanced across the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, and elsewhere. Different countries have different grievances, but they are all reacting to the same fundamental problem: people are losing confidence in political establishments that transferred too much sovereignty away from the nation-state. Le Pen fits directly into this trend because her opposition to Brussels has always been central to her political appeal. National Rally no longer advocates withdrawing France from the European Union or abandoning the euro, but Le Pen continues to argue that France must regain sovereignty from EU institutions. That is what terrifies the establishment far more than all the rhetoric about the “far right.” France is one of the pillars holding the European project together, and a French president willing to challenge the authority of unelected bureaucrats in Brussels would pose a threat to European centralization that Hungary or Slovakia simply cannot. The EU was sold to Europeans as an economic union that would facilitate trade and prevent another European war. It has transformed itself into an enormous political bureaucracy regulating energy, agriculture, automobiles, immigration, environmental policy, trade, and increasingly defense and foreign affairs. The average French citizen cannot vote the European Commission out of office. Yet those bureaucrats can impose regulations that directly affect what car he drives, what his electricity costs, how farmers use their land, and what policies his national government is permitted to implement. This is precisely why nationalism has continued gaining ground. The establishment insists that people voting for these parties have somehow become extremists, but perhaps they should look in the mirror. Trump did not create nationalism in America, Brexit did not create nationalism in Britain, and Le Pen did not create nationalism in France. These movements expanded because governments increasingly stopped representing the interests of the people who elected them. France illustrates the trend perfectly. Le Pen received only 17.9% in the first round of the 2012 presidential election. She increased that to 21.3% in 2017 and then 23.2% in 2022. In the presidential runoff, she went from 33.9% against Macron in 2017 to 41.5% in 2022. Now she is polling around 36% before the first ballot is even cast in 2027. You do not need some complicated political theory to understand what is happening. The direction has been underway for more than a decade. The establishment has nevertheless repeatedly attempted to contain nationalist parties rather than address why people are voting for them. Germany constructed its political “firewall” against AfD, whereby the traditional parties refuse cooperation regardless of how many Germans vote for it. Austria’s Freedom Party won the largest share of the vote in its 2024 parliamentary election yet initially found itself excluded while establishment parties attempted to construct a government without it. Millions of Europeans are effectively being told that they are free to vote for whomever they like, provided their vote does not actually change who governs. Romania exposed how dangerous this mentality can become. Călin Georgescu unexpectedly won the first round of the presidential election in 2024 before the Constitutional Court annulled the election amid allegations of campaign irregularities and Russian interference. Georgescu was then barred from participating when the election was rerun. There were legal arguments behind those decisions, but politically the result was extraordinary: the man who won the first election was not permitted to compete in the replacement election. That does not restore confidence in democracy. It destroys it. Now look at Le Pen. Her conviction in the European Parliament assistants case initially included an immediately prohibition on seeking public office that threatened her participation in 2027. Her legal position subsequently changed through the appeals process, leaving her able to run, but France came remarkably close to having the eligibility of its leading opposition candidate determined by the judiciary rather than the electorate. Then there is campaign financing. National Rally has repeatedly struggled to obtain loans from French banks despite representing millions of French citizens. Le Pen was forced to seek financing outside France in previous elections, and Jordan Bardella has again complained about the difficulty of securing French bank financing for 2027. Each institution can offer its own explanation, but voters are not blind when they see the same political movement confronting obstacles from the courts, banks, bureaucracy, media, and traditional parties simultaneously. This is why the latest poll matters. The old strategy is losing its effectiveness. For decades, the French establishment relied upon the Republican Front, whereby parties that despised each other would nevertheless unite in the second round to prevent National Rally from winning. That worked spectacularly in 2002 when Jacques Chirac defeated Jean-Marie Le Pen with more than 82% of the vote. By 2017, Marine Le Pen had increased the family’s runoff vote to nearly 34%. Five years later she reached 41.5%, and now polling suggests the barrier that once made a National Rally presidency virtually impossible is continuing to erode. The establishment should ask WHY instead of trying to devise another method to stop the candidate. People throughout Europe are rejecting governments that demand endless sacrifices for Brussels while ignoring problems at home. They have watched uncontrolled immigration transform communities, Net Zero policies drive up energy costs, sovereign debt expand, taxes increase, and billions flow into foreign wars while governments insist there is no money for their own citizens. Then the same political class lectures voters that choosing anyone who challenges this arrangement represents a threat to democracy. That has been the mistake throughout Europe. The establishment treats nationalist politicians as the cause when they are merely the political manifestation of a much broader collapse in confidence. You can investigate a politician, construct a firewall around a party, deny financing, or prevent coalition participation, but none of those measures addresses why voters abandoned the establishment in the first place. France could become the decisive test because a nationalist victory there would have consequences far beyond French domestic politics. Brussels can isolate smaller states when they resist EU policy, but it cannot treat France as some troublesome peripheral member. If France begins demanding the restoration of national sovereignty, challenging centralized immigration policy, opposing further EU federalization, and refusing to blindly follow Brussels on foreign affairs, the entire political balance of the European Union changes. Nationalism has already returned as a major political force, and France is demonstrating that the trend is continuing. The establishment can attempt to stop individual politicians, but it cannot indefinitely stop millions of people from demanding the return of sovereignty to the nation-state.
